faq.q: How does a radiator heat the room?
faq.a: Mostly by convection. It warms the air next to it, the warm air rises, and a slow circulating current carries heat round the room. A smaller share travels as infrared radiation.
When air warms, its particles move faster and spread apart, so a litre of warm air weighs less than a litre of cool air. The denser cool air sinks and pushes the warm air up.

faq.q: Why are radiators put under windows?
faq.a: Windows are the coldest part of the room. A radiator beneath warms the cold air falling off the glass, which stops chilly draughts along the floor.
asks: Where is the best place for a radiator?

faq.q: Why do radiators have fins at the back?
faq.a: The fins give a much bigger surface area of hot metal, so more air touches it and more heat passes to the room.
asks: What are the zigzag bits behind a radiator?

faq.q: Why is the top of my radiator hot but the bottom cold?
faq.a: If the bottom is cold, sludge may be blocking it; if the top is cold, air is trapped and needs bleeding out through the valve.
asks: Why does a radiator need bleeding?

facts: Despite the name, most of the heat from a typical radiator reaches the room by convection rather than radiation.
A convection current forms because warm air is less dense than cool air.
